title: Are VT codes optimal single-deletion-correcting codes for every length?
credit: Varshamov-Tenengolts (1965), Levenshtein; optimality question recorded by Sloane (2002)
premise_risks: Could be false for some larger n (only n<=11 verified); posed as prove-or-disprove
Object named after people (VT codes) but the question is not a person-named conjecture
plain: A set of binary strings of length n corrects one deletion if no two of its strings can become the same string when each loses one symbol. The Varshamov-Tenengolts code VT_0(n), the strings whose position-weighted sum of 1s is divisible by n+1, is such a code, with about 2^n/(n+1) words. Is VT_0(n) a largest single-deletion-correcting code for every length n?
math: Let $D(n)=\max\{|C|: C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ \mathcal D_1(x)\cap\mathcal D_1(y)=\emptyset\ \forall x\ne y\in C\}$, where $\mathcal D_1(x)$ is the set of length-$(n-1)$ subsequences of $x$. Let $VT_0(n)=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n i x_i\equiv0\pmod{n+1}\}$, so $|VT_0(n)|=\frac{1}{2(n+1)}\sum_{d\mid n+1,\ d\text{ odd}}\varphi(d)\,2^{(n+1)/d}$. Decide whether $D(n)=|VT_0(n)|$ for all $n\ge1$.
